title: Strength to the weary
hook: a later blessing thanks God for giving strength to the tired
tomorrow: The soul you gave me is pure

segments.voice: Yesterday, pokeach ivrim, the blessings for sight, freedom and clothing, borrowed from a psalm. Your line was eyes opened. What did you see that you'd never noticed? Today, the blessing for people who wake up tired. Day five hundred forty-five.

Not everybody wakes up rested. The baby was up at three. The worry was up at four. Some mornings you open your eyes and the first thing you feel is how heavy your arms are. A prayer book that only thanked God for bright, bouncing mornings would leave a lot of people out. So it matters that near the end of the morning blessings, many prayer books carry one that seems written for exactly this person. It isn't in the Talmud's list at all. It came later, and it stuck.
screen: `NOT EVERYBODY WAKES UP RESTED.` → `THE BABY AT THREE.` → `A BLESSING THAT CAME LATER.`

segments.voice: The words are: blessed are you, hanoten laya'ef koach, who gives strength to the weary. The phrase is taken from the prophet Isaiah. In the old Jewish translation, chapter forty: "He giveth power to the faint." A few verses on, Isaiah promises that those who wait for God will renew their strength, and run, and not be weary. The word ya'ef means worn out from effort, the tiredness of someone who has been working or walking a long way. Here's the history. The Talmud's list of waking blessings doesn't include this one. It shows up in the medieval prayer books of France and Germany, and from there it spread. Some authorities hesitated. Rabbi Joseph Karo, author of the Shulchan Aruch, the code of Jewish law, was uneasy about a blessing the Talmud never mentions. But the custom held, and today it's widely said, in many communities as the last of the morning blessings. Look at where it lands. After all the blessings for eyes and legs and clothes, one more line admits something honest: you're up, but you may not be full of energy. The blessing doesn't pretend otherwise. It doesn't say who makes the weary cheerful. It says who gives them strength, enough to begin. Sleep is treated as a gift that restores, and the morning starts by thanking God for what was restored, even if it's only partly.
screen: `HANOTEN LAYA'EF KOACH.` · `FROM ISAIAH 40.` · `NOT IN THE TALMUD'S LIST.` · `ENOUGH STRENGTH TO BEGIN.` · then, large: `STRENGTH TO THE WEARY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest one minute, then begin. Settle, and breathe. Let your shoulders drop. Let your hands go heavy in your lap. Don't try to feel energetic; just admit how tired you actually are, right now, on a scale of one to ten. Then breathe slowly, and feel what's still there under the tiredness: a heartbeat, a breath, enough strength to sit here. If you pray, you can say hanoten laya'ef koach. When the bell comes, start the next thing you have to do, even slowly. The bell holds the time.
Ya'ef. Worn out from effort — the later morning blessing hanoten laya'ef koach gives strength to everyone who wakes up tired, even partly restored.
Your line: enough to begin. Today, notice one tired person near you, and take one small thing off their load: a dish, an errand, a minute of quiet. Day five hundred forty-five.

screen: `DAY 545 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SOUL YOU GAVE ME IS PURE.`

howItsDone: Many Jewish prayer books include the blessing 'who gives strength to the weary' among the morning blessings, often as the last of the series, said at home or at the start of the morning service.

original.note: Hebrew: who gives strength to the weary, from Isaiah 40:29.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful pep talk for the morning.
what it means: an honest blessing for people who wake up tired, thanking God for enough strength to begin.
what a scholar hears: absent from the list in Berakhot 60b, it appears in medieval Ashkenazi rites; Joseph Karo questioned it, and the Ashkenazi custom kept it.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'the great codifier of the sixteenth century' (superlative and date), 'most prayer books' (now 'widely said' / 'many'), and the 'Think about' line.

Joseph Karo's hesitation (Shulchan Aruch / Beit Yosef OC 46) and the Rema's endorsement of the Ashkenazi custom; confirm the characterization 'uneasy' and current Sephardi practice.
